section.title: The Death of Elisha
section.sectionRationale: Israel's kings Jehoahaz and Jehoash both do evil, yet the LORD graciously delivers Israel from Aramean oppression and preserves them for the sake of His ancient covenant. Elisha, dying, gives King Jehoash a final prophetic sign about victory over Aram that the king only half fulfills through weak faith, and even after Elisha's death and burial, a corpse touching his bones is revived, a last, vivid testimony to the LORD's power at work through him to the very end.
section.thesis: Even amid Israel's persistent unfaithfulness, the LORD remains gracious, compassionate, and covenant-keeping, proving through Elisha's final acts, including power flowing from his very bones after death, that the LORD's saving power is not exhausted even when human faith is weak and partial.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Jehoahaz's oppression and the LORD's gracious deliverance, verses 1 to 9; Jehoash's reign summarized, verses 10 to 13; Elisha's final prophecy and the king's half-hearted response, verses 14 to 19; and Elisha's death, the revived corpse, and Jehoash's recovered cities, verses 20 to 25.

units.label: Jehoahaz's oppression and the LORD's grace
units.note: the LORD gave Israel a deliverer

verses.text: In the twenty-third year of the reign of Joash son of Ahaziah over Judah, Jehoahaz son of Jehu became king of Israel, and he reigned in Samaria seventeen years.
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD and followed the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit; he did not turn away from them.
So the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He delivered them continually into the hands of Hazael king of Aram and his son Ben-hadad.
Then Jehoahaz sought the favor of the LORD, and the LORD listened to him because He saw the oppression that the king of Aram had inflicted on Israel.
So the LORD gave Israel a {{yasha|deliverer}}, and they escaped the power of the Arameans. Then the people of Israel lived in their own homes as they had before.
Nevertheless, they did not turn away from the sins that the house of Jeroboam had caused Israel to commit, but they continued to walk in them. The Asherah pole even remained standing in Samaria.
Jehoahaz had no army left, except fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers, because the king of Aram had destroyed them and made them like the dust at threshing.
As for the rest of the acts of Jehoahaz, along with all his accomplishments and his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
And Jehoahaz rested with his fathers and was buried in Samaria. And his son Jehoash reigned in his place.
In the thirty-seventh year of the reign of Joash over Judah, Jehoash son of Jehoahaz became king of Israel in Samaria, and he reigned sixteen years.
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD and did not turn away from all the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit, but he walked in them.

As for the rest of the acts of Jehoash, along with all his accomplishments and his might, including his war against Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
And Jehoash rested with his fathers, and Jeroboam succeeded him on the throne. Jehoash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel.

units.label: Elisha's final prophecy
units.note: my father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel

verses.text: When Elisha had fallen sick with the illness from which he would die, Jehoash king of Israel came down to him and wept over him, saying, "My father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel!"
Elisha told him, "Take a bow and some {{chets|arrows}}." So Jehoash took a bow and some arrows.
Then Elisha said to the king of Israel, "Put your hand on the bow." So the king put his hand on the bow, and Elisha put his hands on the king's hands.

"Open the east window," said Elisha. So he opened it and Elisha said, "Shoot!" So he shot. And Elisha declared: "This is the LORD's arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Aram, for you shall strike the Arameans in Aphek until you have put an end to them."
Then Elisha said, "Take the arrows!" So he took them, and Elisha said to the king of Israel, "Strike the ground!" So he struck the ground three times and stopped.

But the man of God was angry with him and said, "You should have struck the ground five or six times. Then you would have struck down Aram until you had put an end to it. But now you will strike down Aram only three times."

units.label: Elisha's death and the revived corpse
units.note: the man was revived and stood up on his feet

verses.text: And Elisha died and was buried. Now the Moabite raiders used to come into the land every spring.

Once, as the Israelites were burying a man, suddenly they saw a band of raiders, so they threw the man's body into Elisha's tomb. And as soon as his body touched the {{etzem|bones}} of Elisha, the man was revived and stood up on his feet.
And Hazael king of Aram oppressed Israel throughout the reign of Jehoahaz.

But the LORD was gracious to Israel and had {{racham|compassion}} on them, and He turned toward them because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And to this day, the LORD has been unwilling to destroy them or cast them from His presence.
When Hazael king of Aram died, his son Ben-hadad reigned in his place.

Then Jehoash son of Jehoahaz took back from Ben-hadad son of Hazael the cities that Hazael had taken in battle from his father Jehoahaz. Jehoash defeated Ben-hadad three times, and so recovered the cities of Israel.

yasha.gloss: Deliverer or savior, from the root yasha, to save. The LORD graciously raises up an unnamed deliverer for Jehoahaz's oppressed Israel, the same root behind the name Joshua and, ultimately, Yeshua, Jesus, the name meaning the LORD saves.

chets.gloss: Arrow. Elisha's enacted prophecy with bow and arrows becomes a test of the king's own earnestness; the number of times Jehoash strikes the ground with the arrows directly determines the extent of Israel's future victories, showing how prophetic promise and human response are woven together.

etzem.gloss: Bone. That resurrecting power flows even from Elisha's etzem after his own death is among the most striking miracles in the Old Testament, a final testimony that the power at work through Elisha's ministry always belonged to the LORD, not to any inherent quality in the prophet himself.

racham.gloss: Compassion or mercy, from the root associated with a mother's womb, rechem, conveying deep, tender care. The LORD's racham toward persistently unfaithful Israel is rooted not in their merit but in His own ancient covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, a mercy that outlasts generations of national failure.

basic.context: Two more evil kings of Israel, Jehoahaz and his son Jehoash, continue Jeroboam's idolatry, yet the LORD graciously delivers oppressed Israel from Aramean domination when Jehoahaz seeks His favor, and preserves the nation for the sake of His ancient covenant despite ongoing unfaithfulness. As Elisha lies dying, King Jehoash visits him in tears, and Elisha gives him an enacted prophecy with a bow and arrows: shooting one arrow guarantees full victory over Aram, but striking the ground with the remaining arrows determines how completely that victory will be realized. Jehoash strikes only three times, earning Elisha's rebuke and a limited, partial victory rather than total destruction of Aram. Elisha then dies and is buried, yet even after his death a corpse thrown into his tomb is revived on contact with his bones, a final, vivid testimony to the LORD's ongoing power, and the chapter closes noting Jehoash recovered Israelite cities from Aram just as promised.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative recounting the reigns of two kings and the final acts of a dying prophet; it is not a formula suggesting that striking the ground a certain number of times determines outcomes generally, nor a claim that bones possess inherent magical power. What endures is the LORD's persistent grace toward an undeserving people for covenant reasons, and the sobering truth that half-hearted engagement with God's promises yields only partial results.
basic.originalLanguages: The LORD graciously raises up a yasha, deliverer or savior, for oppressed Israel, the same root behind the name Jesus. Elisha's final prophetic act uses chets, arrows, to test the king's earnestness, and the number of times he strikes determines his victories. Even Elisha's etzem, bones, retain resurrecting power after his death, a vivid testimony that the power was always the LORD's own. And the LORD's racham, compassion, toward persistently sinning Israel flows from His ancient covenant, not their merit.
basic.typology: The unnamed deliverer raised up for oppressed Israel points forward to the ultimate Deliverer, Jesus, whose name itself means the LORD saves, while the corpse revived by contact with Elisha's bones anticipates the far greater resurrection power at work in Christ, who raises the dead not through relics but by His own inherent authority and life.
basic.christ: The unnamed deliverer the LORD raises for oppressed Israel, whose name is never given because the deliverance itself, not the human agent, is the point, anticipates the ultimate Deliverer, Jesus, whose very name declares that the LORD saves, Matthew 1:21. And the astonishing revival of a corpse merely touching Elisha's bones, even after the prophet's own death, anticipates the far greater and complete resurrection life Christ possesses in Himself, John 11:25, and which He grants freely to all united to Him, needing no relic or intermediary but His own living presence.
basic.god: God remains gracious and covenant-keeping even toward a persistently unfaithful people, delivering Israel not because they deserve it but because of His ancient promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He also honors even partial, hesitant faith with real though limited blessing, showing that half-hearted obedience yields real but incomplete results, while His own power, on vivid display even from a dead prophet's bones, is never in question.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 15:18-21 and 17:7-8 give the ancient covenant with Abraham that 13:23 explicitly cites as the reason for God's continued mercy toward Israel. Matthew 1:21 names Jesus as the one who will save His people from their sins, the fulfillment of the deliverer pattern raised up here. Acts 19:11-12 records handkerchiefs from Paul carrying healing power, a similar though lesser display of God working through physical means associated with His servants.
basic.oneStory: Even amid generations of persistent idolatry, God remains faithful to His ancient covenant, raising up deliverers and displaying astonishing resurrection power even from a dead prophet's bones, previewing the ultimate Deliverer, Jesus Christ, whose name means salvation and whose own resurrection life, unlike Elisha's borrowed and temporary display of power, is permanent, complete, and freely given to all who trust in Him.

context.literary:
The chapter is built in two matched halves that share a structure without repeating content. Verses 1 to 9 summarize the reign of Jehoahaz using the standard formula, evil king, divine anger, foreign oppression, then a plea and deliverance; verses 10 to 13 give the briefest possible notice of his son Jehoash's reign, only four verses, before the narrative slows dramatically for the extended, personal scene of verses 14 to 21. That slowing is itself a literary signal: after two kings dispatched in thirteen verses combined, Elisha's deathbed and the tomb miracle receive eight verses of close, almost cinematic attention, the camera lingering on a weeping king, a bow and arrows, a window opened east, and finally a corpse tossed hastily into a tomb.

The final two verses, 24 and 25, function as a coda that answers the prophecy just given: Jehoash strikes Ben-hadad three times and recovers Israelite cities, exactly as many times as he struck the ground, verse 19, turning what could have felt like a private, almost incidental miracle scene into a hinge on which real subsequent history visibly turns. The chapter closes the entire Elisha narrative cycle that opened in chapter 2 with the same emotional gesture, a witness crying "my father, my father," bracketing roughly fifty years and a dozen intervening chapters of ministry with matching grief.
context.historical:
Jehoahaz's army reduced to fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers, verse 7, describes a catastrophic military collapse, and this remnant force reflects Aram's real and sustained dominance over Israel through Hazael's long reign, consistent with the broader regional picture of ninth century Aramean strength.

Elisha's illness and death close a ministry that began at the Jordan roughly fifty years earlier, 2 Kings 2, making him a fixture across the reigns of at least five kings of Israel. A king weeping at a dying prophet's bedside and addressing him as "my father" reflects real royal deference to a figure whose word had shaped policy and battle outcomes for decades, not mere sentiment.

Reviving the dead through contact with a holy man's remains, while unique in its specific occurrence here, fits a broader biblical assumption that God's power could attach itself to a prophet's person even after death, comparable in kind, though not degree, to garments and shadows later carrying healing associations with Elijah, Elisha, and the apostles, 2 Kings 2:8, 2 Kings 2:14, Acts 19:11 to 12. Moabite raiders using the spring season for incursions, verse 20, matches the agricultural calendar of the region, when roads dried and armies could move freely after the winter rains.
context.canonical:
This chapter closes the Elisha cycle in a way that deliberately answers its opening. In chapter 2, Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's spirit and receives it visibly, parting the Jordan with Elijah's own mantle; here, at his death, that same spirit empowered ministry proves potent even without the man himself, power flowing from bones rather than a living hand. The narrative arc that began with one prophet succeeding another ends with the succeeded prophet's power outliving him entirely.

Jehoash's cry, "my father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel," verse 14, is not a new expression but a word for word echo of Elisha's own cry over the ascending Elijah, 2:12. The author intends readers who have followed the whole cycle to hear that quotation and recognize Elisha now standing in Elijah's place, honored by a king exactly as he once honored his own master.

Later Scripture returns to this era through the prophets contemporary with Jehoash's own son Jeroboam II. Amos and Hosea, ministering only slightly later in the very century framed by this chapter, will describe Israel's continuing sin in far harsher terms than the sympathetic tone of Elisha's tears here, showing how a chapter that ends on hopeful notes, deliverance and recovered cities, sits right before the moral reckoning those prophets soon pronounce. The pattern of a servant of God whose power and blessing outlast his own life anticipates the New Testament's confidence that Christ's own resurrection life, unlike Elisha's borrowed and temporary display, needs no relic or tomb to transmit it, since He Himself remains alive to give it directly to all who come to Him, Hebrews 7:25.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wants readers to hold two truths side by side without collapsing either one. First, that Israel's kings, generation after generation, kept walking in Jeroboam's sin, verses 2 and 11, with no exception offered for either Jehoahaz or Jehoash. Second, that the LORD kept acting graciously toward this same unrepentant nation anyway, raising up a deliverer, verse 5, and honoring even Jehoash's partial, hesitant faith with real, if limited, victories, verses 18 to 19 and 25. Neither truth is allowed to erase the other.

The final miracle at Elisha's tomb serves the author's larger purpose across the whole Elijah-Elisha cycle: to make unmistakably clear, at the very last possible moment, that every act of power across fifty years of ministry belonged to the LORD and not to the prophet as such. A corpse reviving from contact with bones that can no longer move, speak, or intend anything, is the author's way of stripping away any lingering suspicion that Elisha himself, rather than the God who sent him, was the true source of his ministry's power.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is a historical account of one unrepeated miracle and one specific enacted prophecy; it establishes no ongoing practice of seeking healing through contact with a holy person's remains, nor a general rule that striking an object a fixed number of times determines the size of any blessing. Scripture nowhere commends relic veneration on the strength of this account, and the text itself treats the miracle as remarkable precisely because it is unprecedented, not because it models a repeatable technique.

What the chapter does establish as an enduring pattern, beyond this single episode, is the connection between wholehearted engagement with a promise already given and the fullness of what is eventually received. Jehoash was never told a fixed number of times to strike; his own restraint set his own ceiling. That principle, that half measures answered with half hearted effort still yield real but limited results, transfers naturally to prayer, obedience, and any promise a believer has been given without a stated limit, Ephesians 3:20, James 4:2.

debates.question: Why did Elisha grow angry at Jehoash for striking the ground only three times, verses 18 to 19?

views.label: The action tested and exposed the king's own limited resolve and faith
views.case: Elisha's instruction, strike the ground, was open ended, inviting the king to respond with wholehearted eagerness; Jehoash's decision to stop after only three strikes, rather than continuing until told to stop, revealed a restrained, half committed engagement with the promise, which then determined the limited scope of the resulting victories.

views.label: A prophetic enacted parable illustrating the general principle of proportionate faith and blessing
views.case: The episode functions less as a literal test of Jehoash's personal character and more as an enacted lesson, similar to other prophetic sign acts in Scripture, illustrating a broader spiritual principle that the extent to which God's people engage His promises in faith and effort shapes the extent of the blessing they experience, without necessarily being a definitive verdict on Jehoash's entire character.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree the episode teaches that eager, full engagement with God's promises yields fuller blessing than cautious, limited engagement, whether read as a specific test of this king's heart or a broader enacted principle for God's people generally.

debates.question: Was the unnamed deliverer of verse 5 a foreign king or a domestic figure such as Jeroboam II?

views.label: An Assyrian king, most likely Adad-nirari III
views.case: A westward campaign by an Assyrian king against Damascus around this period would have weakened Aram's grip on Israel from entirely outside Israel's own action, fitting the LORD using an unwitting foreign power as His instrument, much as Cyrus later serves as the LORD's instrument for Israel with no personal devotion, Isaiah 45:1.

views.label: A domestic figure within Israel, such as Jehoash's own later recovery of cities
views.case: Since the text never names the deliverer and the immediate narrative sequence moves directly to Jehoash's own victories over Ben-hadad, verses 24 to 25, and Jeroboam II's larger recoveries in the next chapter, some read the deliverance as unfolding gradually through Israel's own later kings rather than pointing to any single external figure.

debates.bearing: Either way, the text's own silence about who or what the deliverer was is deliberate; the author wants the LORD's initiative, not the identity of His instrument, to be what readers remember, exactly as verse 4 attributes the deliverance to the LORD hearing Jehoahaz rather than to any strategy of Israel's own.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond yasha, chets, etzem, and racham, a few more features of the Hebrew deserve notice. Verse 4 says Jehoahaz "sought the favor of the LORD," an idiom built from chalah, to be weak or entreat, joined to panim, face, literally to entreat the face of the LORD. The same idiom describes Moses interceding for Israel, "Moses sought the favor of the LORD his God," Exodus 32:11, and later becomes standard biblical language for humble, urgent prayer, "seek My face," 2 Chronicles 7:14. Jehoahaz's entreaty, brief as the text records it, uses the same words Scripture elsewhere reserves for its most earnest intercessors.

Elisha's declaration over the arrow shot east, verse 17, calls it "the LORD's arrow of victory," built from teshuah, deliverance or salvation, the same root, yasha, behind the word "deliverer" just used of verse 5. The military image and the theological vocabulary are the same word family: the arrow itself is named salvation before it ever strikes anything, so that the outcome is announced as certain in the very naming, even though the king's own follow through, striking the ground, will determine how completely that certain salvation gets realized.

Elisha is called "the man of God," ish ha'elohim, in verse 19, a title used of him consistently since chapter 4 and of Elijah before him, marking a recognized prophetic office rather than a private reputation; when this same man of God "was angry," qatsaph, at the king's half hearted response, his anger functions as an authoritative verdict, not a personal mood, since the title itself claims to speak for God.

Finally, Jehoash's cry in verse 14, "my father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel," reproduces Elisha's own cry over Elijah in 2:12 word for word in the Hebrew, avi avi rekhev yisrael u-farashav. Such an exact, deliberate quotation across eleven chapters and roughly fifty narrated years is a literary signature the translation can only gesture toward; two men, two generations, and one identical cry mark the same office passing through the same words. The verb Elisha uses for Jehoash's action, nakah, to strike, verses 15 to 19, is the ordinary word for a military blow, so that a king striking dust with an arrow shaft is deliberately described in the same vocabulary as striking an enemy army, collapsing the enacted sign and the real battle into one continuous act of faith or its absence.

typology.type: An unnamed deliverer raised up to rescue oppressed Israel from Aram
typology.fulfillment: The LORD raises up a deliverer, yasha, whose name the text withholds entirely, verse 5, so that the deliverance itself, not the human agent, receives all the attention. Centuries later an angel names a child before His birth specifically because of what He will do, "you are to give Him the name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins," Matthew 1:21, Jesus being built from the same Hebrew root left unnamed here. Where Israel's deliverer in this chapter is anonymous and his rescue partial, lasting only until the next oppressor, Jesus is named, permanent, and saves completely rather than temporarily, Hebrews 7:25. The type is genuine but modest: an unnamed rescue from one enemy anticipates a named Rescuer from every enemy.

typology.type: Resurrecting power flowing from a dead prophet's remains
typology.fulfillment: A dead man revives the instant his body touches Elisha's bones, verse 21, the LORD's power still active in a prophet who can no longer will, speak, or intend anything himself. Christ's own resurrection life works by an entirely different, greater logic: He does not merely transmit power passively from a grave but declares Himself, while fully alive, "I am the resurrection and the life," John 11:25, and gives that life directly rather than through contact with remains. The type still falls meaningfully short: Elisha's bones stayed in the tomb and the revived man eventually died again, while Christ's own body did not stay in its tomb at all, and those united to Him will not die a final death, John 11:26.

typology.type: A dying prophet's final act of intercession for the king's future
typology.fulfillment: Elisha, dying, still acts on the king's behalf, guiding his hands to the bow and speaking a word of guaranteed victory before rebuking his half measures, verses 15 to 19, a prophet's last recorded act being intercession for someone else's future. Yet Elisha's intercession, however faithful, ends with his death; Christ's does not. "Because Jesus lives forever, He has a permanent priesthood, therefore He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them," Hebrews 7:24 to 25. What Elisha could offer only once, at the very end of a long ministry, Christ offers continuously and without any ending.

typology.type: A prophetic succession cry, repeated word for word across two generations
typology.fulfillment: Jehoash's cry over the dying Elisha repeats Elisha's own cry over the ascending Elijah word for word, 2:12 and 13:14, marking one prophetic office passing to the next across a whole generation. Both Moses and Elijah, the giver of the law and the greatest of the prophets, appear together on the mount of transfiguration only to vanish, leaving Jesus alone, while the Father's voice declares, "this is My beloved Son, listen to Him," Matthew 17:3 to 5. The long line of prophets succeeding one another, each mourned and honored in turn, finds its intended terminus not in a further successor but in the Son to whom every prophet, including Elisha, was always pointing, Hebrews 1:1 to 2.

study.christ:
Where Jehoash's faith proves partial, three strikes instead of five or six, Christ's own obedience to every purpose of the Father is never partial or hesitant. Gethsemane shows the difference starkly: facing something far heavier than a king's uncertain campaign, Christ prays not for release but "not as I will, but as You will," Matthew 26:39, and carries that resolve through to the cross without ever stopping short. Jehoash's three victories over Ben-hadad, real but capped by his own restraint, are a small, human scale picture of what limited obedience yields; Christ's finished work, "it is finished," John 19:30, is what unlimited obedience accomplishes.

The scene of a king weeping over a dying man he calls father anticipates, in miniature, the far greater grief and greater hope bound up in Christ's own tears. Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb, John 11:35, not because He lacked power to raise him but because death itself, even a death He was about to reverse, remained an enemy worth grieving. Where Jehoash's tears could only accompany a prophet's death that even a later miracle could not undo, Elisha still died and stayed dead, Christ's own tears at a tomb preceded a raising that pointed forward to His own resurrection, the first fruits of a reversal Elisha's ministry could only foreshadow, 1 Corinthians 15:20 to 23.

The covenant reason given for the LORD's mercy, "because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob," verse 23, finds its full outworking in Christ, the seed in whom that covenant's blessing finally reaches "all the families of the earth," Genesis 12:3, Galatians 3:16. Every act of grace toward faithless Israel across this chapter, the deliverer raised up, the arrow of victory, even the tomb's astonishing power, rests on a promise older than any king in this chapter, a promise this chapter's whole plot serves rather than originates, and one Christ alone brings to its intended completion.

Even the geography of Elisha's final sign points forward. The window opened toward the east, verse 17, the direction of Aram and of the very Eden humanity was driven from, Genesis 3:24, casts the arrow of victory as a small reversal of exile's direction, a shot fired back toward the place of loss. Christ's own victory is not aimed at recovering one border but at reopening the way east into the garden itself, so that the flaming sword barring Eden gives way at last to a gate no conquest of Ben-hadad could ever unlock, Revelation 22:14.
study.god:
This chapter puts the LORD's anger and the LORD's compassion in the closest possible proximity without resolving the tension into something simpler. Verse 3 says His anger burned against Israel and delivered them to Hazael; verse 23 says He was gracious to them and had compassion on them and would not yet destroy them. Both statements describe the same LORD toward the same unrepentant nation within twenty verses of each other, refusing readers any easy summary of God as only wrathful or only kind.

God is willing to work real, if limited, good through weak instruments. Jehoash never becomes a wholehearted king; verse 11 flatly repeats that he, like his father, did not turn from Jeroboam's sin. Yet this same unremarkable king receives a genuine prophetic word, real victories, and recovered cities, showing that the LORD's purposes do not wait for spotless agents before moving forward through them, even while their own incompleteness still costs them something real.

God's compassion here is explicitly backward looking rather than forward earning; it rests on "His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob," a promise made centuries earlier to men who are not even mentioned again in this chapter's own events. This is a striking claim about how God's mercy operates across time, an ancient promise still governing His present dealings with a generation who never renewed it and gave Him no fresh reason to keep it.

Finally, God's power in this chapter is emphatically not tied to visible strength. Israel's army is reduced to dust, verse 7, and yet the LORD still delivers; Elisha's body is a corpse in a tomb, and yet the LORD's power still raises a stranger through it. Across the chapter, national weakness and a prophet's death are precisely the settings in which the LORD demonstrates that His capacity to save was never dependent on the visible strength of either the nation or its holiest man.

crossReferences.note: The ancient covenant with Abraham, made long before Israel existed as a nation and resting on God's own oath rather than on any performance by Abraham's descendants, is the covenant verse 23 names directly as the reason the LORD had not yet destroyed Israel despite generations of continued idolatry.

The LORD's self declared character, compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion, supplies the vocabulary verse 23 draws on directly. Israel's persistent idolatry across this whole chapter tests every clause of that ancient declaration, and the declaration holds.

Elijah's original commission included anointing Hazael over Aram and Jehu over Israel, both of whose descendants now fill this chapter, Hazael's son Ben-hadad and Jehu's grandson Jehoash. A charge given at Horeb generations earlier is still working itself out to its last details here.

Jehoash's cry over the dying Elisha, my father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel, is not his own invention but a verbatim echo of Elisha's own cry over Elijah's ascension, marking one prophetic office passing visibly into the next.

Where the deliverer of verse 5 goes unnamed so that attention falls entirely on the LORD's own initiative to save, the angel's instruction to name Mary's son Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins, gives that same saving initiative a permanent name and a permanent, once for all rescue.

Moses and Elijah appear briefly with Jesus on the mount of transfiguration only to vanish, leaving Him alone as the Father declares Him His beloved Son to be heard, the long prophetic line, including Elisha's, finding its intended goal in the Son rather than in any further successor.

Many priests died and had to be replaced, exactly as prophets like Elisha eventually died; Christ's permanent priesthood, since He lives forever, means He never needs replacing and can save completely those who come to God through Him.

Christ's declaration to Martha that He Himself, while fully alive, is the resurrection and the life goes well beyond anything Elisha's story claims for Elisha; power that merely lingered in a dead man's bones is answered by a Person who holds resurrection life in Himself and gives it to whoever believes.

Handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched Paul carried healing to the sick and freed the demon possessed, an apostolic era echo of the same principle at work in Elisha's tomb, that God's power can attach itself to what has been in contact with His servant, without that object ever becoming the true source of the cure.

study.oneStory:
This chapter sits at a hinge in Israel's long decline. The kings before it, from Jeroboam onward, have compounded a single unaddressed sin for roughly a century and a half; the kings after it, through chapters 14 to 17, will finally exhaust the LORD's patience, ending in Samaria's fall and Israel's exile among the nations. Chapter 13 is one of the last places in that long story where mercy, not yet judgment, gets the final word, Jehoahaz delivered, Jehoash granted victories, a corpse raised, even while every underlying cause for judgment remains fully in place.

The chapter's peculiar final miracle, resurrection power flowing from a dead man's bones, becomes a small, physical parable for the whole book's larger argument: the power that has driven this entire story was never Elijah's or Elisha's own, and it does not expire when they do. That same truth carries the reader past Israel's coming exile toward a much larger horizon, since the God who raised a stranger through contact with bones is the same God who will one day raise His own Son bodily and permanently, and through Him will finally undo death itself rather than merely reversing it once.

The new creation answers this chapter completely. There death will not merely be interrupted by a passing miracle at one particular tomb; it will be swallowed up forever, and "there will no longer be any curse," Revelation 21:4, 22:3. The man revived by Elisha's bones died again eventually; those raised in Christ will not. This chapter's astonishing but temporary reversal is a signpost pointing toward the permanent reversal the whole story has been moving toward since a promise was first spoken in a garden, Genesis 3:15.

quiz.q: Why did the LORD raise up a deliverer for oppressed Israel under Jehoahaz?

options.text: Because Jehoahaz sought the LORD's favor and the LORD saw the severe oppression Aram had inflicted on Israel.
options.note: Verses 4 to 5 give this exact reason for the LORD's gracious deliverance.

options.text: Because Israel had fully repented of all their idolatry.
options.note: Verse 6 explicitly states they continued in Jeroboam's sins despite this deliverance, so full repentance had not occurred.

options.text: Because Jehoahaz had defeated Aram in battle himself.
options.note: Israel's army had been devastated by Aram, verse 7; the deliverance came from the LORD's initiative, not a military victory Jehoahaz achieved.

options.text: No deliverance occurred, and oppression continued unabated.
options.note: The text explicitly states the LORD provided a deliverer and Israel escaped Aram's power.

quiz.q: What enacted prophecy did the dying Elisha give King Jehoash, and how did the king respond?

options.text: He had the king shoot an arrow symbolizing victory over Aram, then strike the ground with the remaining arrows, but the king stopped after only three strikes rather than continuing further.
options.note: Verses 15 to 18 record this exact prophetic sign and the king's limited response.

options.text: He told the king to fast for seven days before battle.
options.note: The specific enacted prophecy involved a bow, arrows, and striking the ground, not fasting.

options.text: The king refused to participate in the prophecy at all.
options.note: Jehoash did take the bow and arrows and struck the ground three times, engaging with the prophecy, even if only partially.

options.text: The king struck the ground until Elisha told him to stop.
options.note: The text states the king himself stopped after three strikes, which is precisely what provoked Elisha's anger.

quiz.q: What was Elisha's response to the king's limited action, and what result did it produce?

options.text: Elisha grew angry and told him that because he stopped at three strikes, he would only defeat Aram three times rather than completely destroying them.
options.note: Verse 19 records Elisha's rebuke and the specific limited outcome that followed.

options.text: Elisha praised the king for his complete and total victory over Aram.
options.note: Elisha's response was one of rebuke for an incomplete action, not praise for a total victory.

options.text: Elisha declared that no victory over Aram would ever occur.
options.note: A real, if limited, victory was still promised and later fulfilled in verse 25, not a total denial of victory.

options.text: Elisha gave no response to the king's action at all.
options.note: The text explicitly records Elisha's anger and specific verbal rebuke.

quiz.q: What extraordinary event occurred after Elisha's death and burial?

options.text: A dead man's body, thrown into Elisha's tomb while fleeing raiders, was revived to life the instant it touched Elisha's bones.
options.note: Verses 20 to 21 record this exact, striking miracle occurring after Elisha's death.

options.text: Elisha's tomb was found completely empty with no body inside.
options.note: The text describes a body being placed into and reviving within Elisha's tomb, not an empty tomb.

options.text: Nothing unusual happened after Elisha's burial.
options.note: A specific, extraordinary revival is explicitly recorded following his burial.

options.text: The raiders themselves were struck dead near the tomb.
options.note: The miracle concerned the revival of a deceased Israelite man, not the death of the raiders.

quiz.q: Why does the text say the LORD continued to show grace and compassion to Israel despite their persistent idolatry?

options.text: Because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, being unwilling to destroy Israel or cast them from His presence.
options.note: Verse 23 gives this exact covenantal reason for the LORD's ongoing mercy.

options.text: Because Israel had fully abandoned all idol worship by this point.
options.note: The text consistently notes Israel's continued idolatry throughout this chapter, not full abandonment of it.

options.text: Because Jehoash had personally torn down the Asherah pole.
options.note: The Asherah pole is noted as still standing in Samaria, verse 6, not removed by any king in this passage.

options.text: The text gives no reason for God's continued mercy.
options.note: Verse 23 explicitly and specifically grounds this mercy in God's ancient covenant with the patriarchs.

questions: The LORD raised up a deliverer for Israel not because they deserved it but because He saw their genuine distress. Where in your own life do you need to remember that God's help flows from His compassion, not your merit?

Jehoash stopped striking the ground after only three times, and it cost him a fuller victory he could have had. Where might you be settling for a smaller measure of God's promise because you stopped short of full, eager engagement?

Elisha's power to raise the dead continued to flow even after his own death, showing the power was always God's, not his own. How does recognizing that all spiritual power ultimately belongs to God, not to any human instrument, shape how you view gifted or influential people in your own life?

Israel kept sinning generation after generation, yet God's compassion for them was rooted in an ancient promise rather than their current behavior. How does knowing God's covenant faithfulness does not depend on your consistency encourage you today?

This chapter closes an entire era of dramatic prophetic ministry with one final, unexpected miracle. What faithful work has God been doing in your life over a long season that you might not yet see the full fruit of?

translationNotes.note: The deliverer's identity is left unspecified in the text; various interpreters have suggested Adad-nirari III of Assyria, whose campaigns against Aram around this period would have relieved pressure on Israel, though the text itself credits the LORD alone as the source of deliverance.

Jehoash's cry over the dying Elisha, my father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel, deliberately echoes Elisha's own earlier cry over the ascending Elijah in 2:12, marking the honor Elisha had come to hold in Israel.

The number of strikes against the ground directly and symbolically determined the number of subsequent victories over Aram, later fulfilled precisely as Jehoash defeated Ben-hadad three times, verse 25.
